title: Session mistakes
summary: Review cookie attributes and browser storage choices for a session token.

scenario.briefing: A proposed login stores an opaque session token in a cookie and also in localStorage. Review the attributes and storage choice before the feature ships.

objectives.description: Identify unsafe session cookie attributes and storage.

hints: An HttpOnly cookie is not readable by page scripts.
Secure limits the cookie to HTTPS. SameSite limits cross-site sending.
localStorage is readable by scripts, so an XSS flaw can steal the token.
Add HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite, and keep the web session out of localStorage.

misconceptions.description: Treating localStorage as a secure credential store.
misconceptions.feedback: Any script running in the page can read localStorage. An XSS bug then becomes session theft.

misconceptions.description: Believing HttpOnly alone protects a session.
misconceptions.feedback: HttpOnly blocks script reads, but transport security, SameSite, and CSRF protection are also part of session safety.

sections.title: Cookies carry attributes with consequences
sections.body: HttpOnly prevents page scripts from reading a cookie. Secure restricts it to HTTPS. SameSite controls whether cross-site requests include it. These attributes reduce different risks; none is a complete session design by itself.

sections.title: XSS changes the threat model
sections.body: If an attacker can run script in the page, localStorage is readable. HttpOnly cookies are not. Server-side verification, revocation, and CSRF protection still matter because a browser can be tricked into sending requests.

vocabulary.definition: A cookie attribute that blocks access from page scripts.
A cookie attribute controlling cross-site requests.
Cross-site request forgery, where a browser is tricked into sending an authenticated request.

findings.label: Storing the token in localStorage exposes it to page scripts.
The claim that CSRF is irrelevant is fully correct.

verdicts.label: Reject until cookie attributes, storage, and CSRF handling are safe

steps.explanation: The cookie is script-accessible, transport-unprotected, and cross-site sendable. The token is also copied into localStorage.

steps.title: Session safety

statements.label: HttpOnly prevents page scripts from reading the cookie.
Secure restricts the cookie to HTTPS.
SameSite reduces some cross-site request risks.
localStorage is a safe place for session tokens.

steps.explanation: Session safety combines cookie attributes, transport security, CSRF defenses, and care about script access.
